step2.heading: Start with your browser: how many of 50 ad and tracker requests does it let load?
step2.instruction: Press Run in the browser you use most; you get a result with or without a blocker. It sends 50 ad, analytics, social and beacon test requests to our own server and counts the ones that load. About 5 seconds.

step3.red: 26 or more of the 50 loaded. On other sites, trackers that match these patterns would load too and see your visit. DNS filters such as Pi-hole score zero here by design.
step3.amber: 6 to 25 of the 50 loaded: something filters, with gaps. Look at which of the four groups leaked; analytics, social pixels or beacons point to a missing tracker list.
step3.green: 45 or more of the 50 were stopped, so common tracker patterns get little from this browser. Your connection and passwords, the other two, are separate free checks.

step4.line: On a computer, the free fix is a blocker extension with EasyList and EasyPrivacy both on. On an Android phone, the free Incognito Browser app has an ad blocker built in, and Incognito Pro adds ad and tracker blocking that stops many analytics and social trackers before they load.

step1.quote: A browser mode that prevents local storage of browsing history, cookies, and form data on your device, but doesn't hide your activity from websites, ISPs, or network administrators.

step2.heading: Open this in a private window and a normal one, then compare the address
step2.instruction: Nothing to type. Load it in a private window, then a normal one: each shows the address and rough location every site receives, and any address WebRTC hands out, within seconds.
step2.button: Compare my address in both windows

step3.red: WebRTC gives pages a second public address, private window or not. On a VPN, that's likely your real one getting around the tunnel.
step3.amber: In private windows too, WebRTC lists more than the address at the top, and none of the extras is a leak: local addresses, a network neighbour, or one it can't compare.
step3.green: A private window doesn't change this address: without a VPN it's your ISP's or network's, and every site sees it. Only a VPN or a proxy changes it.

step3.green: WebRTC added nothing outside your own address block; a neighbour in it is your network. If the top address changes with Private Relay off, the relay was hiding yours.

step1.label: The term
step1.quote: A cryptographic system using two mathematically linked keys: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption, enabling secure communication without sharing secrets.

step2.heading: This tool uses one shared passphrase. See why key pairs replaced that
step2.instruction: Encrypt a line with a passphrase here, the older way: one secret locks it. Copy the block, switch to Decrypt, and the same secret opens it - the secret your recipient would need too.

step3.green: Locked with a shared secret. Your recipient needs the passphrase, which you must get to them another way; a public key never needs hiding.

step1.label: The term

step1.label: The term
step1.quote: Malicious software that encrypts a victim's files or locks their computer system, demanding payment (usually cryptocurrency) in exchange for restoring access to the data.

step2.instruction: Paste a link from an email you're unsure about, such as a shared file, invoice or delivery notice. Nothing is downloaded or opened; the result shows each hop it can decode and the host at the end.

step3.green: Unwrapped and untagged: the link goes straight to the host shown. That rules out wrapping, not ransomware; open files only if you expected them.

step4.line: Free first: a backup drive kept unplugged, which ransomware on your computer can't reach. Incognito Pro's URL Safety Checker works at the way in, reading an email link's address before you tap for look-alike brands, odd endings, raw IPs and shorteners.

step1.label: The term
step1.quote: A legal right that allows individuals to request the deletion or removal of personal data about them from online platforms, search engines, and databases under certain circumstances.

step3.red: Under half marks. Two of this entry's three examples are social posts and a professional profile; if Social Media is a weak bar, lock it down alongside any request.
step3.amber: Removal is never automatic, whatever your 50 to 79 says: requests face a balancing test against public interest, so data you never publish is data you never argue over.
step3.green: The past is what's left at 80 or more: old results like the bankruptcy article in this entry's first example, which a request to Google can address.

step1.label: The term

step2.heading: A sandbox is only as strong as its last update. Check your browser's version
step2.instruction: Nothing to type: the User Agent Analyzer shows your browser's version and flags it if it's outdated. Browser updates regularly fix flaws that let code slip out of the sandbox.

step3.red: Outdated, per the result. Security fixes, sandbox ones included, arrive in updates; this version is behind, so install the latest.
step3.amber: Current, with a Client Hints box. The sandbox keeps scripts off your files, yet they can still request your full version, OS version and, on Android, phone model.
step3.green: Current and plain, no Client Hints. The sandbox keeps a page away from your files; what your browser tells sites, like screen size and time zone, is a separate question.

step1.label: The term

step2.instruction: VPN off, if you use one. In Chrome or Firefox, press the VPN-off button, turn on secure DNS with a named provider and run it again: the resolver networks should change. VPN users, then add a VPN-on run.

step3.green: Nothing leaked with the VPN on: your ISP's resolver didn't answer. Keep secure DNS on for the times the VPN is off, so lookups stay encrypted then too.

step1.label: The term
step1.quote: A cryptographic technique that allows multiple parties to jointly compute a function over their inputs while keeping those inputs private from each other.

step2.heading: See the building block: data you hand over that others can't read
step2.instruction: Encrypt a line with a passphrase in the Text Encryption Tool here. It isn't multi-party computation, only the basic idea under it: what you share stays unreadable without the key.

step3.red: Sealed still: 'Decryption failed' says the passphrase or the block didn't match, and nothing more. In multi-party schemes each party holds only a share of the data.
step3.amber: Decrypted, and the whole input is visible to whoever holds the passphrase. Multi-party computation is designed so no single party ever sees it.
step3.green: Encrypted: you can hand this over and keep the words private. Multi-party computation goes further: several parties get one answer without seeing each other's inputs.

step4.line: The everyday version is free: share the answer, not the raw data, like the one figure asked for instead of a whole screenshot. A photo can share more than you meant; Incognito Pro's Photo Metadata Viewer lists the photo's GPS, camera and time fields and saves a clean copy.

step1.label: The term
step1.quote: A digital identity model where individuals control their personal data and credentials without relying on centralized authorities like governments or corporations.

step2.heading: Your credentials today are passwords and second factors. Score them
step2.instruction: Two of the quiz's 12 questions ask how you manage passwords and which two-factor login you use, from none to a hardware key. The Accounts row scores both. About 2 minutes.

step3.red: Below 50. If passwords or two-factor login made your recommendations, start there: no question in the quiz carries more weight than those two.
step3.amber: Middling, 50 to 79: an Accounts row short of full marks means a password or second factor below the top answer, a manager with unique passwords or a hardware key.
step3.green: However strong your passwords at 80 or more, each service still keeps its own record of you; self-sovereign identity would put that proof in your hands.

step3.green: 45 or more blocked in this session. Session cookies keep you signed in and go on close; persistent cookies are the ones that stay behind.

step1.label: The term

step1.label: The term

step3.green: Nothing in this link singles you out, and it goes straight to the host shown. The personal touches are in the email itself, so verify the request too.
